newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba goes against White House transition proposal.
newsitem.headline: Cuba goes against White House transition proposal.

text.p: Cuban President Fidel Castro's government has mounted a vigorous campaign against a recent White House document outlining technical and financial aid Havana might receive in return for radical political change.
National Assembly President Ricardo Alarcon appeared on state-run television on Monday night to denounce the report and vow Cubans will "never become slaves again."

His remarks capped days of attacks on the document by Cuban officials and the state-run media. The government has treated the report, issued one week ago, as yet another U.S. assault on Cuba's sovereignty.

"Through supposed aid to Cuba, Cubans would pay for a plan that would destroy them and demolish Cuba as a nation, to take it into slavery," said Alarcon, who has also given interviews to local television and the youth communist newspaper Juventud Rebelde.

The White House report, with a preface by U.S. President Bill Clinton, dangles the prospect of billions of dollars in foreign aid to Cuba if it dumps its communist system and moves toward a market economy. It details technical assistance such as help in restructuring political institutions that Washington thinks Cuba would need in a transition period.

It was issued to comply with a section of the Helms-Burton law, legislation passed last year that toughened the 35-year-old U.S. embargo against Cuba. Castro and Foreign Minister Roberto Robaina have also attacked the report, saying Cuba was not for sale to the highest bidder.

Detailed criticism was left to Alarcon, a former foreign minister and ambassador to the United Nations who, apart from Castro, often is Cuba's leading spokesman on U.S. affairs. He peppered his remarks with unusually harsh criticism of the U.S. president, asking sarcastically if Clinton aimed to become mayor of Miami -- home to a large part of the Cuban American community who are critical of Castro.

Or perhaps Clinton aspired to be an adviser to Jesse Helms, Alarcon said, referring to the Republican Senate Foreign Relations Committee chairman who co-authored the legislation signed by Clinton last March after Cuban fighters shot down two private U.S. aircraft flying near the island.

Alarcon went through the document page by page to expose what he called an effort to "sow confusion" among Cubans. He said Cuban authorities would take the report for futher discussion among workers, students, farmers and women.

Details of the document have been publicised by the United States government-funded Radio Marti aimed at Cuban listeners. But Alarcon sought to dispel any notion the prospect of large sums of money could tempt Cubans suffering economic hardships.

Even if such money did arrive, it would be at a huge cost, he said. The $4 billion to $8 billion worth of loans, grants and other assistance the document says might go to Cuba was not actually promised by the United States, Alarcon said.

He said Cuba also was expected to come up with huge sums as a condition to better relations with the United States -- for example by reaching agreement on compensation for expropriated property estimated to be worth $6 billion in registered U.S. claims alone.

The United States envisaged Cuba cutting its public health care system, introducing private education and coping with large numbers of people laid off after state enterprises were privatised, he warned.
